us-chase.conditions: Domestic case: a student living in New Haven keeps a Chase account with a US address with no special condition. G 'Change of Address'): 'You must promptly notify us of any change in the address(es) associated with your account. If you change your address to an address located outside the United States, or we determine that you are residing outside the United States, we may close your account.' So for a customer living abroad, keeping the account is conditional and at Chase's discretion. The bank-initiated closure clause (sec. VIII 'Closing Your Account'): 'Either you or we may close your account at any time for any reason or no reason without prior notice.' The agreement also says ACH/RTP may not be used on behalf of someone who is not a US resident.
us-chase.usResidentPolicy: Not applicable as a restriction: Chase is a US bank and US persons are its main customers. It collects a TIN, which for a US person means a W-9 SSN/ITIN. The restriction runs the other way: foreign addresses and foreign residence can lead to closure (see conditions).
assumptions: SLATE assumes a Chase customer who moves abroad keeps the account only until Chase acts on the foreign address, which the agreement allows it to do at any time and without notice. SLATE does not model a fixed grace period, because none is published.
SLATE assumes the 3% Foreign Exchange Rate Adjustment applies to the standard Chase Total Checking account. Premium tiers that waive it are not modelled.

ca-rbc.conditions: RBC's Personal Deposit Account Agreement (s.24 'Address or Residency') requires the client to 'immediately notify us' of any change of address or residency, and to report any change of tax residency 'within 30 days'; 'failure to provide a valid self-certification under FATCA or CRS will result in the temporary restraint of your Account until such time as it is provided'. RBC can still close the account at its discretion: s.6 lets it 'suspend, freeze, or restrict access to, restrain, block, or terminate your right to use your Account ... for any reason in our discretion, including, without notice' (e.g. unsatisfactory operation, contrary to policies, required by law). After 12 months without transactions the account goes inactive; a $0 inactive account is closed without notice, and the balance goes to the Bank of Canada after 10 years.

An account with a missing self-certification is restrained, not described as closed. RBC also markets RBC Bank (U.S.) accounts to Canadians who study in the US, which assumes that keeping the Canadian RBC account is normal.
assumptions: SLATE assumes RBC keeps a Canadian account open for a holder who moves to New Haven, provided the holder reports the move and the change of tax residency within 30 days, because the agreement requires notice and self-certification but contains no clause that closes an account because the holder lives abroad.
SLATE assumes RBC Online Banking and the Mobile app keep working from the US, since RBC publishes no geographic restriction and markets cross-border banking to students in the US.
SLATE assumes RBC can close the account at any time without notice under s.6, so the account carries a small discretionary closure risk rather than a fixed notice period.

If the address is outside the UK, Barclays says it will contact the customer to close the current/savings account. Its student FAQ says accounts stay open while the customer is UK-based and close once they leave. A Yale student (multi-year stay) fits none of the exceptions. Notice: Barclays' page says only it will 'give you as much notice as we can'; the personal terms' general clause (quoted in Financial Ombudsman decisions) lets Barclays close a personal account on at least two months' notice. For accounts opened on or after 28 April 2026 the statutory minimum is 90 days (see countries.GB). Alternative: Barclays International Banking (offshore) needs at least £100,000 in savings/investments (£250,000 for a relationship manager).
gb-barclays.usResidentPolicy: Not published for UK retail accounts. Residence outside the UK is itself the closure ground, so a US resident is closed out whatever their nationality. Nothing is published about refusing US persons (citizens) who live in the UK.
assumptions: SLATE assumes closesWithNoticeDays = 60 (two months) for a Barclays account opened before 28 April 2026, from the general personal-terms clause as quoted by the Financial Ombudsman; Barclays' current personal terms PDF was not read directly.
SLATE assumes a Yale student on a multi-year course does not qualify for the 'six months or less' temporary-absence exception, so Barclays closes the account once a US address is registered.

Customers moving abroad must tell Lloyds and change their address, in branch per Lloyds help. Lloyds-site snippets say overseas-addressed customers keep receiving statements and cards, that Lloyds offers new savings accounts only to UK residents, and that out-of-policy non-UK-resident savings accounts are closed and repaid by sterling cheque. In 2020–21 Lloyds Banking Group closed UK accounts of customers resident in some EU countries for Brexit licensing reasons; that was country-specific and did not cover the US. Notice: Financial Ombudsman decisions quote Lloyds' terms as giving 'at least 2 months' notice when ending an agreement, and record a 65-day closure notice to a customer living abroad. Lloyds' site blocked automated fetching (Cloudflare error 1007), so this rests on search snippets of lloydsbank.com pages and PDFs.

Lloyds Bank International publishes that its International Plus Account is not available to US, Canadian or Hong Kong residents 'due to regulatory requirements'. Its terms note that 'a US citizen is treated as US tax resident' for reporting.
assumptions: SLATE assumes Lloyds keeps the current account of a customer who moves to the US and notifies the address change, but may close it with notice at its discretion, because its terms say 'may not be able to keep your account open' rather than 'will close'.

gb-natwest.conditions: NatWest publishes no closure rule for customers moving outside the EEA. Its Brexit hub says that for EEA-resident customers 'our aim is to continue to provide you with the same service ... where we are permitted to do so', and that it closed accounts of many Netherlands residents because of Dutch law. Its support centre (search snippet) says that 'in most cases, there will be no change to the products and services you use if you move abroad', but packaged-account benefits (e.g. insurance) cannot be used while living overseas. Customers must not keep a UK address on file if not UK-resident. Notice: 'As stated in our Terms and Conditions, we're required to give you 60 days' notice of our intention to close your account.' Expat alternative: NatWest International (Jersey) International Select account, minimum balance £25,000, £8 monthly fee, residents of eligible countries only.
gb-natwest.usResidentPolicy: not published. Nothing found on refusing or closing accounts of US residents or US persons. Whether the US is eligible for NatWest International's International Select account is not stated on its page (it uses an eligibility checker).
assumptions: SLATE assumes NatWest keeps a UK current account open for a customer who moves to the US and registers the US address, because NatWest publishes no closure rule outside the EEA and says that 'in most cases' nothing changes.
SLATE assumes closesWithNoticeDays = 60 for an account opened before 28 April 2026, from NatWest's own statement of its terms; 90 days applies to accounts opened on or after that date.

gb-hsbc.conditions: HSBC UK, 'Leaving the UK checklist', on keeping the UK account: 'Although you're allowed to do so, it only makes sense if you'll be using the account regularly'. Dormant accounts may be frozen or closed. Some account features may not be available while living outside the UK, and HSBC says to 'speak to your bank about your plans before you move and check any residency requirements'. An HSBC UK notice (search snippet, about EEA residents under CRD6 Article 21c) says existing products 'will remain unchanged' but 'While you live outside the UK, HSBC UK Bank plc won't offer you any other ... products or services'. Terms (effective 6 July 2026): HSBC may close accounts 'by giving you at least two months' notice or any longer period required by regulation'. It may close straight away if, among other things, 'You haven't given us information that we've asked for about your tax situation' or 'You weren't entitled, or aren't entitled any longer, to ... have your account'. A Basic Bank Account may be closed on two months' notice if 'You're no longer legally resident in the UK.'
gb-hsbc.usResidentPolicy: not published for HSBC UK retail. The terms say that if HSBC believes the customer may be tax resident in another country it may disclose information to HMRC, which may pass it to another government under an agreement. HSBC Expat lists the USA among countries where it can help open accounts. Its FAQ says nothing about US-person restrictions.
assumptions: SLATE assumes HSBC UK keeps the current account of a customer who moves to the US (kept = true), because HSBC publishes 'you're allowed to do so', while it stops offering new products and may close on notice like any account.

SLATE assumes closesWithNoticeDays = 60 for an account opened before 28 April 2026; the 6 July 2026 terms defer to 'any longer period required by regulation' (90 days for accounts opened on or after 28 April 2026).

ie-aib.conditions: AIB publishes no rule that closes a personal current account when the holder moves abroad. Its help pages let a customer change their address to a foreign country in the app or Internet Banking (Services > My Details > select country). The customer must tell AIB if their country of tax residence changes so that AIB can update its tax records. Some AIB products are limited to Irish residents: the Personal Sterling Current Account 'is only available to personal customers resident in Ireland'. Nothing equivalent is published for the euro personal current account. Bank-initiated closure: AIB's current account terms say AIB may close a personal current account by giving at least two months' notice (general termination clause; PSD2 framework-contract rule, S.I. 6/2018).
ie-aib.nonResidentFee: not published (no non-resident surcharge in the material read). From 1 July 2026 the standard personal current account fee is EUR 6 per month, replacing EUR 4.50 per quarter plus transaction fees. AIB Student and Student Plus accounts are exempt (AIB press release of 18 March 2026 and the 'Changes to fees and charges' page, read via search snippets because aib.ie returned HTTP 403).
ie-aib.usResidentPolicy: AIB does not publish a refusal or closure policy for US persons. It publishes FATCA obligations: AIB must report accounts held by US citizens and US tax residents to Irish Revenue, which exchanges the data with the IRS. Account opening requires a tax certification that establishes whether the holder is a US citizen and where they are tax resident. If the self-certification conflicts with other data held (for example a US address), AIB asks for a 'CRS/FATCA Reasonable Explanation Form' with supporting documents.
assumptions: SLATE assumes AIB keeps a euro personal current account open for a customer who moves to the US and registers a US address, because AIB publishes a foreign-address change path and no residency condition for that account.
SLATE assumes no non-resident surcharge applies beyond the standard EUR 6 monthly fee, because none is published.

SLATE assumes a student who held an AIB Student/Student Plus account keeps the fee exemption only while AIB's eligibility for that account holds. AIB's eligibility rules for continuing study abroad were not found.

PTSB's terms say that accounts held by non-residents (as defined by the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997) 'must be operated in accordance with statutory conditions and banking regulations' and that 'an additional form must be completed where a non-resident Account is required'. A customer who becomes non-resident may therefore need to complete a non-resident form, which is also the route to DIRT exemption. PTSB must report these under CRS and FATCA to the Revenue Commissioners.

is-landsbankinn.conditions: Landsbankinn publishes no rule that closes an account when the holder moves abroad. Its general terms require the customer to give name, kennitala, legal domicile and, where relevant, residence or tax domicile ('skattalega heimilisfesti'), and to keep them current. Its US-tax page requires everyone tax resident outside Iceland to register their foreign TIN with the bank. Access abroad depends on electronic ID (see access). Bank-initiated closure: 'Bankanum er heimilt að segja upp rammasamningi samkvæmt skilmálum þessum með tveggja mánaða uppsagnarfresti' (the bank may terminate the framework contract with two months' notice) (Almennir viðskiptaskilmálar 1532-06, June 2023, art. on termination). The bank may also end the relationship without notice for law or terms breaches, AML risk, reputational risk, or where the relationship 'does not fit its risk policy'.
is-landsbankinn.nonResidentFee: not published. The price list has no monthly current-account fee. The debit card annual fee is ISK 790 (free under 18), and debit card transactions cost ISK 18 each (free under 18; 150 free a year for ages 18–24) (Verðskrá effective 25 August 2026, items 2.1.1 and 2.5.1).
is-landsbankinn.usResidentPolicy: No refusal of US persons is published. Landsbankinn's 'Bandarísk skattamál' page says that under the Iceland–US information-exchange agreement (FATCA) the bank must in certain cases collect IRS W-forms. A W-9 is required from anyone born in the US, with US citizenship, or with US residence/address. A W-8BEN is required from non-US persons with US-source income. Forms are valid for three years.
assumptions: SLATE assumes Landsbankinn keeps a current account open for a holder who moves to the US and registers a foreign tax residence and TIN, because no closure-on-emigration rule is published.

SLATE assumes a holder without an Icelandic passport (for example a foreign national who lived in Iceland) cannot set up e-ID remotely from the US, and so loses app/online access unless they already hold a working Auðkenni app or an Icelandic SIM e-ID.
SLATE assumes item 9.2.1.1 (ISK 700) is the fee for an incoming USD payment. The price list also shows ISK 400 for 9.2.1.3, and how the two lines combine is not published.

fr-bnp-paribas.conditions: BNP Paribas publishes a separate non-resident price for an active euro current account, so an existing account can continue after the holder stops residing in France, but at non-resident pricing. The holder must tell the bank about changes (the convention says the client must provide 'sans délai' any information, change or supporting document useful for the account, including a change of address) and complete a FATCA/CRS self-certification. The bank can close the account at any time with 2 months' notice (convention clause: 'La Banque peut, à tout moment, clôturer le compte ... la Banque accorde au Client un délai de préavis de 2 mois'), or without notice for seriously reprehensible behaviour. BNP Paribas has a dedicated 'filière Non-Résidents' (international branches) for expatriates. Inactive accounts (L312-19 CMF) cost 30 EUR a year.
fr-bnp-paribas.nonResidentFee: Tenue de compte actif en euros for clients not resident in France: 10 EUR/month if resident in the EU or an EAI (CRS) country; 15 EUR/month if resident in a non-EAI country. The brochure's footnote (3) says: 'Les États-Unis ne font pas partie des pays EAI', so a US resident pays 15 EUR/month. Reduced by 2.50 EUR/month when an 'Esprit Libre' package fee is charged. The same page lists 'Tenue de compte pour les clients âgés de moins de 25 ans: Gratuit', but does not say whether that also waives the non-resident fee.
fr-bnp-paribas.usResidentPolicy: The bank publishes no refusal or closure policy for US persons. The convention says FATCA and the OCDE CRS standard require the bank to identify its clients' tax residences and 'plus spécifiquement d'identifier les US Person', collecting a self-certification and supporting documents. The bank is also a US Qualified Intermediary (QI). In the 2019-2021 'Américains accidentels' episode, the press and a 2021 parliamentary question reported that at least one major French bank notified US-born clients that their accounts would be closed if no US TIN was provided. The bank was not named in official sources.

fr-societe-generale.conditions: SG publishes a quarterly 'frais de gestion administrative pour les clients non-résidents', so accounts of non-residents continue at extra cost. The client must tell SG 'dès que celui-ci survient' of any change of tax-residence country, from French tax resident to non-resident, and of acquiring US citizenship or a green card. SG then collects a new self-certification. Before a permanent move abroad, SG asks the client to contact their adviser to update postal address and phone. SG may close the account on its own initiative by registered letter 'moyennant le respect d'un délai de préavis de 2 mois, sans avoir à en indiquer le motif'. It may close on the same terms if the client refuses to provide documents required for its legal or regulatory obligations, and with no notice for seriously reprehensible behaviour or abnormal account operation (CG art. 'Clôture à l'initiative de la Banque').
fr-societe-generale.nonResidentFee: Frais de gestion administrative pour les clients non-résidents (capped at one charge per client per quarter, on top of account-keeping fees): EU residents 25 EUR/quarter; residents of an EAI country 50 EUR/quarter; residents of a non-EAI country 75 EUR/quarter. Exempt: clients under 25, Banque Privée clients, inactive accounts, Généris holders, Services Bancaires de Base holders. The standard account-keeping fee is 7.65 EUR/quarter, exempt under 25 and with JAZZ/Sobrio etc. A footnote reads '(1) Exonération pour les non-résidents', but the item it attaches to is unclear in the extracted text. SG does not say whether the US counts as EAI.
fr-societe-generale.usResidentPolicy: SG publishes no blanket refusal or closure of US persons. The CG say SG must identify clients who are US taxpayers under FATCA or residents of CRS (NCD/EAI) countries and report them via the French tax administration to the IRS or the residence country. Under CMF L564-1, a bank that cannot identify a holder's tax residences and TINs 'n'établit pas de relation contractuelle'. Refusal to provide required documents is a stated ground for closure with 2 months' notice. The client must report acquiring US citizenship or a green card.
assumptions: SLATE assumes SG treats the US as a non-EAI country (75 EUR/quarter), since the US is not a CRS participant. BNP's brochure says so explicitly but SG's does not, and LCL treats the US as EAI (which would mean 50 EUR/quarter).
SLATE assumes the under-25 exemption means a student aged 24 or under pays no non-resident administrative fee.
SLATE assumes transfer delivery time to the US is 1-3 business days, since SG does not publish it.
SLATE assumes SG would ask a US-person client for a W-9 and others for a W-8BEN. The CG name only the tax-residence self-certification.

fr-lcl.conditions: LCL prices accounts of clients resident outside France, so they can be kept. The fee depends on residence and on whether the client 'domicilie ses revenus chez LCL' (has income paid in). Online-banking access is suspended if mail comes back 'NPAI'/'PND' until the new address is given and proven, so the address must be kept up to date. A FATCA/EAI self-certification is mandatory. LCL's account convention was not retrieved. Bank-initiated closure therefore falls under the statutory minimum of 2 months' notice (CMF L312-1-1).
fr-lcl.nonResidentFee: Tenue de compte, client résidant hors de l'Union Européenne (per account per quarter): free for a deposit or Compte Sur Livret account of a resident of an EAI country who has income paid in at LCL; 40.00 EUR/quarter for an EAI-country resident who does not; 80.00 EUR/quarter for residents of other countries. LCL's footnote says 'les États-Unis et le Maroc sont également considérés comme des pays EAI', so a US resident pays 0 or 40 EUR/quarter. Exempt: clients under 26, LCL Initial subscribers, droit au compte accounts and inactive accounts. For comparison, French residents pay 10 EUR/quarter if no income is paid in.
fr-lcl.usResidentPolicy: LCL publishes that 'toute personne née aux États-Unis est un citoyen américain et donc un contribuable américain'. US citizens or tax residents must provide a W-9 (US taxpayers) and the self-certification (the page lists W-8BEN for individuals). 'LCL n'est pas autorisé à entrer en relation ou à ouvrir de nouveaux comptes à des clients refusant de fournir les attestations requises.' For existing clients with discrepancies, LCL asks them to resubmit forms (declaration.fatca@lcl.fr). No published closure of US persons who comply.
assumptions: SLATE assumes LCL's bank-initiated closure notice is 2 months, the statutory minimum in CMF L312-1-1. LCL's account convention itself was not found.
SLATE assumes a student with no income paid into LCL pays 40 EUR/quarter, and pays nothing if under 26.
SLATE assumes foreign-currency (USD) transfers have to be ordered through the branch, because the online CG describe online transfers outside SEPA as euro transfers.
SLATE assumes the 2026-01-01 tariff remained in force through 2026-10-16. A later 2026 LCL tariff (moneyvox 'tarifs-2026-c') exists and was not read.

fr-credit-agricole.conditions: Crédit Agricole d'Île-de-France (CADIF) publishes no non-resident account fee and no rule closing accounts on departure, so the account continues on the convention's terms. The Crédit Agricole convention template requires a tax-residence self-certification, which may be asked for again after opening 'en cas de changement de circonstances'. The template allows the bank to end the convention 'à tout moment en respectant un préavis de deux mois', or immediately for serious anomalies. That convention is the national CGL_CPT_FUSIONNE text, read from the copy published by Crédit Agricole de La Réunion. The CADIF-specific convention was not found.

fr-credit-agricole.usResidentPolicy: Crédit Agricole publishes that it must know whether a client is 'citoyen ou résident américain au sens de la législation FATCA (US Person)'. Before opening, the client must give their US TIN. The bank reports identity, balances and interest to the French tax administration for the IRS, and must report a client to the IRS if US indicia are found and not rebutted. The FATCA page adds that each US Person must obtain a TIN and give it to financial institutions. No published blanket refusal or closure of US persons. Third-party sites claim CA accepts Americans 'case by case', which is not official.

SLATE assumes CADIF's own convention carries the same 2-month bank-closure clause as the national Crédit Agricole template (read from the La Réunion copy), which is also the statutory minimum.
SLATE assumes the scanned tariff's figures are read correctly. They came from OCR of a scanned PDF (online international transfer 15 EUR minimum up to 15,000 EUR; ATM outside euro 3 EUR; card 2.50%).

de-deutsche-bank.conditions: No Deutsche Bank document read says the account ends when the customer moves abroad. Its address-change form (Auftrag zur Adressänderung, form code 250403) lets the customer give a foreign registered address and tick 'Steuerausländer (Ich habe in Deutschland weder einen Wohnsitz, auch keinen Nebenwohnsitz, noch meinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt)'. The same form says the account continues unchanged and that all agreed terms and conditions stay in force. The customer must report the new address and the change in tax residency. de-deutsche-bank.nonResidentFee: No separate non-resident fee published. The standard model prices apply: db AktivKonto EUR 6.90 a month, db BestKonto EUR 13.90 a month. 'Das Junge Konto' (EUR 0.00) needs an EU registered address, so a US-resident student pays the AktivKonto price.
de-deutsche-bank.usResidentPolicy: Not published. Deutsche Bank does not say that it refuses or closes current accounts of US persons or US residents. Its FATCA/CRS self-certification (Selbstauskunft) asks about US citizenship, a green card and US birthplace, and requires an IRS Form W-9 from US citizens and US tax residents. It also says the bank may not open newly requested accounts without a valid tax self-certification (§3a(2) FKAustG).

SLATE assumes the online banking app and BestSign work from the US, because Deutsche Bank publishes no geographic or app-store restriction.

es-santander.conditions: No Santander page found on an existing resident customer moving abroad. Nothing published says existing accounts of US residents/US persons are closed. Spain reports US persons' accounts to the AEAT, which passes them to the IRS (Spain-US FATCA IGA, Model 1).

jp-mufg.conditions: MUFG publishes a dedicated non-resident service, 'Global Direct' (グローバルダイレクト), for customers who leave Japan 'with a plan to return' (帰国予定のあるお客さま) for one of: an overseas posting from a domestic employer, work at a Japanese embassy/consulate, STUDY AT A SCHOOL ABROAD (海外の学校への留学), or as accompanying family. It must be applied for in person at a branch at least 10 bank business days before departure (15 if Mitsubishi UFJ Direct is opened at the same time); 'customers who have already left Japan cannot newly apply' (出国済みのお客さまは、本サービスを新規にお申し込みいただくことはできません). Students must bring a certificate showing study period, school name and school address (e.g. admission letter, 入学許可証). Foreign nationals may apply but must also submit a residence card (在留カード), special permanent resident certificate, or a certified copy of the resident register. Customers moving to an OFAC-sanctioned country cannot apply. Once abroad, investment trusts, mortgage applications and some other transactions are unavailable to overseas residents; the address change for a move abroad (出国) must be done at a branch, not online, and is impossible online if the customer holds investment trusts, public bonds or general zaikei savings. The Japanese-national vs foreign-national distinction: under the Foreign Exchange Act a Japanese national becomes a non-resident on leaving to stay abroad 2+ years (or after 2 years abroad); a foreign national is presumed a non-resident unless working at an office in Japan or 6+ months after entry, so a foreign national who leaves Japan becomes a non-resident immediately. MUFG's ordinary deposit rules (普通預金規定, as of 2026-04-01) require non-Japanese depositors 'residing in Japan' to evidence a lawful status and period of stay and let the bank restrict withdrawals and other transactions once the notified period of stay has expired. Bank-initiated closure clause: the bank may suspend or close the account 'by notifying the depositor' for listed causes (illegal/AML/sanctions use, false KYC, organized-crime ties, inappropriate continuation); closure takes effect when the notice is dispatched to the registered name and address, 'regardless of whether it arrives' (到達のいかんにかかわらず…発信した時に解約). No notice period is stated. Accounts opened on/after 2021-07-01 that go 2+ years unused (and hold no other assets/loans) incur an 'unused-account management fee' of JPY 1,320/year, and if the fee cannot be debited the bank may close the account by notice.
jp-mufg.nonResidentFee: Global Direct: JPY 300/month (non-taxable), debited on the 18th of the following month from the Mitsubishi UFJ Direct representative yen account; JPY 330/month incl. consumption tax for customers who remain Foreign-Exchange-Act residents (e.g. embassy staff). Separately, the unused-account management fee of JPY 1,320/year applies to accounts opened from 2021-07-01 that are unused for 2+ years and hold no other assets.
jp-mufg.usResidentPolicy: MUFG publishes a FATCA page: when opening an account 'or when moving to the United States' (米国への転居をされる際など) it may ask for documents to establish whether the customer is a US taxpayer ('US person etc.': US citizens, anyone born in the US, green-card holders, and anyone residing in the US, with the substantial-presence day test spelled out: 31+ days this year and 183+ days weighted over 3 years). US persons' name, address, account number, TIN, balance and interest are reported to the IRS with the customer's consent (情報開示に関する同意書). If the customer does not cooperate with the FATCA check, a new account cannot be opened, but 'customers who already hold an account may keep it as it is' (口座をそのままお持ちいただけます), though account information may be passed to the IRS via the National Tax Agency on treaty-based request. Nothing published says MUFG closes accounts of US residents or US persons.
assumptions: SLATE assumes a Japanese-national Yale student who leaves Japan for a 4-year degree (so a Foreign-Exchange-Act non-resident) and applies for Global Direct before departure keeps the account at JPY 300/month; one who leaves without applying keeps a domestic-terms account only until the bank learns of the overseas address, after which online international transfers are unavailable and the bank may restrict the account.

SLATE assumes a foreign national who lived in Japan and leaves to study can keep the account only through Global Direct (which MUFG opens to foreign nationals with a residence card and a return plan); without it, once the registered period of stay expires the bank may restrict withdrawals and other transactions under the deposit rules, which in practice means the account should be closed before leaving.
SLATE assumes the ordinary MUFG cash card cannot be used at US ATMs (MUFG publishes overseas ATM use only for the debit card).
SLATE assumes a bank-initiated closure under the deposit rules can happen with no notice period (effective on dispatch), so closesWithNoticeDays is left null rather than 0.
SLATE assumes MUFG withholds 15.315% on a non-resident's deposit interest unless a treaty form is accepted; nothing published says MUFG processes treaty claims for deposit interest.

assumptions: SLATE assumes that a resident current account held in any of the ~230 other countries and territories is kept on a conditional basis after its holder moves to the US to study. The bank may keep it, convert it to a non-resident account, restrict it, or close it under its general closure clause. Birthplace or citizenship alone grants nothing.

SLATE assumes that in the EU/EEA a bank may end a resident basic account when the holder is no longer legally resident in the Union (Payment Accounts Directive 2014/92/EU, Art. 19(2)(d)) with at least two months' written notice (Art. 19(4)). Under PSD2 (Directive 2015/2366, Art. 55(3)) a bank may end an open-ended payment-account contract with at least two months' notice if the contract allows it. SLATE uses 60 days as the EU/EEA notice default and has no default for countries outside the EU/EEA.

SLATE assumes that a holder who becomes a US person (US citizen, green-card holder, or a resident alien after the F-1 five-calendar-year exemption ends) is reported to the IRS by a foreign bank in any of the 114 jurisdictions on Treasury's FATCA IGA list. It also assumes some banks in those jurisdictions refuse or close accounts of US persons, as GAO-19-180 documented, and models this as a non-zero closure risk rather than a rule.

SLATE assumes that an F-1 nonresident alien who is not a US citizen or green-card holder is not a US person, so FATCA does not make their home account reportable to the IRS. The home bank may still ask for a CRS self-certification of the new tax residence. The US does not take part in CRS, so a declared US tax residence produces no CRS exchange to the US.

SLATE assumes that, where a country's banks charge non-residents a monthly account fee, the amount is not published in a form SLATE can verify for the ~230 countries. Non-resident fee is 'not published' and set to null by default, never invented.

SLATE assumes that an outgoing SWIFT transfer from a bank in any of these countries to a US account carries a sending-bank fee that SLATE has not researched country by country, plus possible correspondent and receiving-bank deductions and an FX margin. SLATE does not invent a per-country number. As a calibration only, the FSB's 2024 KPI report puts the global average cost of retail P2P cross-border payments at 2.6% and of a USD 200 remittance at 6.4% (USD 500: 4.3%), against G20 targets of 1% and 3%. Receiving US banks charge $0–$15 for an incoming international wire (Chase $15/$0, BofA $15, Wells Fargo $0, Citi $15, Capital One 360 none listed).

SLATE assumes that bank deposit interest paid to a non-resident is taxed at source at the country's domestic rate when no tax treaty applies, and at the treaty-reduced rate (the OECD Model Article 11(2) caps it at 10% of the gross interest) when a treaty with the US applies and the bank has the holder's residence certification. Many countries exempt bank deposit interest paid to non-residents entirely, as the US does under IRC 871(i)(2)(A). The domestic rate is not researched country by country for the ~230 countries and is 'not published' in SLATE until it is.

SLATE assumes that 131 jurisdictions on the OECD AEOI commitments list (last update 30 September 2026) exchange CRS account information. It also assumes the 42 developing countries listed as 'not asked to commit and that have not yet set a date' (e.g. Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Philippines, Viet Nam) do not exchange CRS data yet. This affects whether the home tax authority learns of a student's account abroad, not whether the home account is kept.

SLATE assumes that KYC refresh and a request for proof of address and a CRS/FATCA self-certification follow a change of residence everywhere. A holder who declares a US address or US tax residence must give a W-9 if a US person, or else a CRS self-certification naming the US as tax residence. A bank that cannot complete KYC on a non-resident may restrict or close the account under its general terms.
